Wenqiu's parents had long since retired from the frontlines, but they still occasionally visited the pastry shop to help her attract customers.
The Five Color Cakes sold best in autumn, though there were steady guests in other seasons too—still, a little promotional shouting was needed.
In winter, they’d claim the cakes stored yang and nourished yin, making them most beneficial to eat in the cold season.
Come spring, their pitch changed: the cakes nurtured liver qi, strengthening the body and ensuring guests fell ill fewer times throughout the year.
By summer, they switched tactics again, declaring the cakes could dispel inner heat.

Gu Wenqiu couldn’t hold back and pulled them aside, telling them to stop reading baseless medical prescriptions.
Her words backfired—now they turned on her, saying her temper was too fiery and she’d do well to eat some Five Color Cakes herself.
Unable to stop them, Wenqiu let them have their way.

As a child, Wenqiu had wondered: with only one Double Ninth Festival a year, why did her parents never seem to rest?
"Because there’s always someone craving them."
Did people really want Five Color Cakes outside the festival?
Wenqiu couldn’t understand. After Lantern Festival, she lost interest in lanterns; once Dragon Boat Festival passed, her Five Color Threads vanished.
Who’d want to celebrate Double Ninth every single day?

Only after taking over the shop did she realize: those who bought cakes together during the festival came alone the rest of the year.
Not every day was Double Ninth, but every day someone remembered the friends they’d shared it with.
Even apart, they carried each other in their hearts.
